speaker: SPEAKER_01
transcript: What does it take to create an equal, just, and joyful world? And how do we sustain ourselves when the work is daunting? I'm Lauren Schiller, creator of InflectionPoint and co-author of the New Book. It's a good day to change the world. We're bringing you a special segment every week of Women's History Month about how we can build a more feminist future and take care of yourself and each other along the way. Today we hear from Sarah McBride about what it takes to advance equality. Sarah became the highest ranking openly trans-official in the country in 2020 when she was elected to the Delaware State Senate. But this wasn't the first time she made history. In 2009, Sarah was a junior at American University when she used her social media platform to come out as a trans woman. She says coming out was the most difficult thing she'd ever done, and realized she wanted to play a larger role in creating an accepting world for more trans people. So, while still in college, she led the way in advocating for the adoption of Delaware's first gender identity non-discrimination bill.

speaker: SPEAKER_00
transcript: For me, it was really difficult because I had always done advocacy from this perspective of advocating for others. And this was in many ways my first experience sort of directly advocating for myself. I had classes Monday and Tuesday night and my mom and I would drive down Wednesday and Thursday to the state legislature for about six months straight. We just literally camped out at legislative hall, day in and day out, meeting with legislators in their offices, but also in the halls, trying to catch them after meetings. It was an exhausting emotional experience. It was an exhausting experience physically. At times, it was a scary experience. I remember at one point, a woman came up to me in the middle of the fight and said, Sarah, have you had the surgery? And I said, I'm sorry, what? She said, have you had the surgery? And I said, ma'am, I don't think that's any of your business. And she said, well, I'll tell you what, if I ever see you in a restroom, I'm going to, and then she described assaulting me. And I then reported that to the capital police officers. It should not be a natural byproduct of advocating for your dignity to then be threatened with violence. But It was also, at the end of the day, I think an inspiring experience for me to be able to stand behind a governor and watch him sign into law that bill and to know that there would be generations of people in our state, people who I will never know, who will benefit from that law. and to know that our government and in many ways our community had just taken a step to affirm our dignity was a hopeful experience and particularly so early on in my coming out in my own journey, I think one that convinced me that this work is worth it.
